extracted.intended_audience: USPTO rulemakers, patent practitioners, and policy makers (patent owners and challengers)
extracted.subtask_description: Formal comments from IEEE-USA on USPTO NPRMs addressing inter partes review, post-grant review, covered business method review, and derivation proceedings, proposing procedural and substantive safeguards for expert evidence, timing, discovery, derivation proof, and rulemaking procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert testimony standards (Daubert applicability)
rubrics_metrics.description: "[T]he spirit of Daubert is applicable to [proceedings before administrative agencies]… 'Junk science' has no more place in administrative proceedings than in judicial ones."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO must ensure expert evidence meets admissibility standards and the integrity of proceedings so they can survive Federal Circuit review. The NPRMs do not address whether Daubert-like standards will apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity to challenge expert testimony / voir dire
rubrics_metrics.description: Will experts be subject to voir dire, Daubert challenges, and the like? If an opening petition relies on expert testimony, it seems unfair and arbitrary for the USPTO to rely on that testimony with no opportunity for the patent owner to challenge it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedures must provide patent owners a fair opportunity to challenge challenger-proffered experts, especially when expert testimony is relied upon at petition stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live trial-type hearings for expert evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Will the USPTO take expert testimony at a live trial-type hearing? This is often crucial to evaluate demeanor and credibility and for the Board to ask its own questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where conflicting expert testimony exists (e.g., on 'on sale'/'public use'), live testimony may be necessary for resolving credibility and factual conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert evidence disclosure requirements (reports and timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: What procedures will be used for disclosure of expert evidence? Will the USPTO use expert witness reports analogous to Fed.R.Civ.P. 26(a)(2)? Or require a challenger to present all evidence supporting the challenge in the opening petition?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If challengers must submit expert evidence in the opening petition, the USPTO must provide a fair opportunity for the patent owner to challenge it; blanket 'no new testimony/evidence' limits in responses (Rules 42.107(c), 42.207(c)) may be extraordinarily unfair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board appointment of neutral experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Will the Board appoint neutral experts, analogous to Fed.R.Ev. 706?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider mechanisms for neutral expert appointment to assist the Board where party experts conflict or where technical issues require neutral analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize inherent unfairness in timing and allow reply extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO should include recognition that challengers often have ample time to build an invalidity case while patent owners face sharply-constrained schedules to defend; locating an appropriate technical expert can take months and should be recognized as good cause for extension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulation or guidance should permit extensions to reply where the patent owner needs time to secure experts and prepare a defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow extended time for reply when foreign 'on sale'/'public use' evidence is involved
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a petitioner raises a 'public use' or 'on sale' challenge, obtaining evidence (e.g., foreign depositions under the Hague convention) can take a year; the global availability of such prior art can create verification difficulties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide time and venue flexibility, and consider this as good cause/interest of justice for extensions to respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to deny petitions relying solely on contested foreign 'on sale' or 'public use' evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 35 U.S.C. §§ 316(b) and 326(b), the USPTO may deny petitions if issues would harm 'the integrity of the patent system' or if the USPTO lacks 'ability … to timely complete proceedings.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IEEE-USA believes this authorizes regulations to deny or strictly scrutinize petitions relying solely on contested foreign on-sale/public-use evidence to prevent abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit patent owner to extend reply on a low showing of good cause
rubrics_metrics.description: One appropriate procedural avenue is to permit the patent owner to extend time for reply to an opening petition on a very low showing of good cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since statutory deadlines run from grant of petition, there appears to be little institutional barrier to permitting such extensions; include in final rule or guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhibit service with citing paper or testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless previously served, any exhibit cited in a paper or in testimony must be served with the citing paper or testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is drawn from the proposed §42.51(1); ensure timely service so parties can vet cited exhibits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-examination of affidavit testimony authorized
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross examination of affidavit testimony is authorized within such time period as the Board may set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate explicit timing and procedures for cross-examination to permit effective challenge to affidavit evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional discovery only upon motion showing 'interest of justice'
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may move for additional discovery. Except in post-grant reviews, the moving party must show such additional discovery is in the interests of justice; the Board may specify conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define standards and conditions for motions for additional discovery; the exception for post-grant reviews must be clarified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery sensitivity to asymmetry of preparation time
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board should be especially sensitive to permitting discovery on issues where the party proffering a position had the luxury of time to fully develop that position and the opposing party needs similar or more time to vet it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historic practice (permitting discovery only where pre-existing evidence suggests need) may not fit the Board’s new world of 'public use' and 'on sale' prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery threshold: 'interest of justice' easily met by patent owner opposing no-document prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulation should make clear that the discovery threshold in 'the interest of justice' is easily carried by a patent owner opposing a no-document prior art challenge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a low threshold for discovery in cases where challenges rely on no-document or difficult-to-verify prior art so patent owners can obtain necessary evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Umbrella Rule estoppel must not exceed statutory authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed 37 C.F.R. § 42.73(d)(3)(ii) would preclude a patent owner from obtaining claims to substantially the same invention, claims that could have been filed in response to any properly raised ground, or amendments denied during trial; this imposes estoppel beyond statutory authorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations must not attenuate statutory rights (e.g., rights under 35 U.S.C. §120 to file continuations) or otherwise exceed Congress’s grant of authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulations must not require preemptive filing of claims to anticipate all contingencies
rubrics_metrics.description: § 42.73(3)(ii) would require a patent owner to contemplate all possible resolutions and preemptively file claims to meet every conceivable contingency, imposing burdens beyond those allowed under the Paperwork Reduction Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid rules that force speculative, burdensome paperwork or claim filings; comply with PRA limitations on paperwork burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not require claim construction in derivation petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed rules require a petitioner to provide a claim construction for every disputed claim in a derivation proceeding (§ 42.405(b)(3)(ii)), which IEEE-USA submits is unnecessary and inappropriate for derivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The existing §42.405(a)(2) showing (same or substantially the same; not patentably distinct) may suffice; consider clarifying form analogous to Rule §41.202(a)(3) instead of adding claim construction requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation rules must require proof of prior conception and communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed Rule §42.405 addresses communication and lack of authorization but ignores that derivation requires proof of earlier conception by the party alleging derivation; mere showing of communication is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include requirements for showing conception (applied to both parties) and communication (applied to the party alleging derivation), consistent with Price v. Symsek and Brand v. Miller.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation showing must be supported by substantial, corroborated evidence (affidavit requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed amendment to §42.405(c): 'A derivation showing is not sufficient unless it is supported by substantial evidence, including at least one affidavit addressing conception and communication of the derived invention and lack of authorization that, if unrebutted, would support a determination of derivation. The showing of conception and communication must be corroborated.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require corroborated affidavits addressing conception, communication, and lack of authorization to meet the sufficiency standard for derivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation petitions should normally not be deferred; define rare deferral circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the statute authorizes the Board to defer action on a petition for derivation until after a patent issues, legislative intent and equity suggest derivation disputes should be resolved before a patent issues and deferral should be the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a rule expressly setting forth the rare circumstances (if any) under which deferral will take place to avoid prejudice to true inventors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation proceedings require a single textual description ('count') to define scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The NPRM proposes no 'count' but requires showing petitioner's claim is 'the same or substantially the same' and 'not patentably distinct' from the invention disclosed to the respondent; without a single textual description ('count') it is unclear how scope will be determined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a 'count' or single textual description of the derived subject matter broad enough to encompass common subject matter of claims in both applications, as in interference practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a two-phase process (scope/count then derivation) in derivation proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: IEEE-USA is skeptical that derivation can be adequately addressed by mere claim comparisons in a single phase; the Board should clarify whether a two-way test will be applied and how scope determinations will be made without a count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement a first phase to examine scope/define derived subject matter and a second phase to determine whether it was derived from the petitioner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement procedures to correct inventor naming under §135(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: The AIA authorizes the Board to 'correct the naming of the inventor in any application or patent at issue' but the proposed derivation regulations fail to implement the statute or provide guidance on 'appropriate circumstances' or process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt explicit rules and processes for correcting inventorship based on derivation determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify treatment of non-patentably distinct claims and remaining patentably distinct claims in derivations
rubrics_metrics.description: NPRM is silent on how non-patentably distinct claims to joint inventions or remaining patentably distinct claims will be treated; this affects the Board's ability to correct inventor naming and define claim status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide mechanisms to determine status of claims of differing scope and the treatment of claims that recite subject matter not conceived or communicated to the deriving party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide procedural avenues to compel discovery from nonparty publishers and applicants for non-patent disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: In fact patterns where A discloses to B, B publishes, C files an application based on B's disclosure, and A later files, true inventor A should be able to compel discovery from nonparty B and party C to show flow of information and derivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement discovery and rebuttal procedures sufficient to allow a true inventor to establish derivation over non-patent disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properly classify rules (legislative vs interpretative; procedural vs substantive) and follow required rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: The NPRMs mischaracterize many provisions as 'interpretative' and 'procedural'; most regulatory text is legislative and enforceable, not interpretative. Misclassification leads to omitted required steps in rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO should correctly classify rules and, where legislative/procedural, use notice-and-comment rulemaking and other required procedures under the APA and applicable case law (e.g., Tafas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not avoid notice-and-comment by mislabeling rules as interpretative
rubrics_metrics.description: The NPRM cites Cooper Techs. for the proposition notice-and-comment is not required, but Cooper's holding on 'procedural' matters is limited and USPTO's later actions (Tafas) bind it to use notice and comment for procedural rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow district/federal circuit precedent and ensure procedural rulemaking is not improperly exempted from notice-and-comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comply with the Paperwork Reduction Act when imposing procedural burdens
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations that require preemptive filing or contemplate all contingencies could impose burdens above 'the least burdensome necessary for the proper performance of the agency's functions,' violating the PRA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess and limit paperwork burdens; ensure any information-collection obligations are justified and, where necessary, submitted for PRA review.
